title: Tencent open-sources Hy4 preview: 770B-parameter MoE with 1M-token context
subtitle: Apache 2.0 license, 49B active parameters per token, an FP8 quantized variant, and an internal blind evaluation that edged GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 on engineering tasks.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Tencent's Hunyuan team released and open-sourced Hy4 preview, a mixture-of-experts language model with 770 billion total parameters and 49 billion active per token, a context window of just over one million tokens, and an FP8-quantized variant for cheaper inference. The weights are on Hugging Face under Apache 2.0. Tencent published API pricing at roughly $0.83 per million input tokens and simultaneously routed the model through OpenRouter and Tencent Cloud TokenHub, so downstream apps can hit it without hosting the weights themselves.

The pattern is the same one Alibaba's Qwen and Zhipu's GLM have been running for a year: release a competitive frontier-class open-weight model, undercut U.S. lab API pricing, and let the ecosystem effects — fine-tunes, third-party hosting, agent frameworks — do the marketing. What is new with Hy4 is that Tencent claims it edges GLM 5.3 and Moonshot's Kimi K3 on internal engineering-task blind evals, which if externally reproduced would put a Chinese open-weight model at parity with the top closed U.S. coding models on the tasks enterprises actually run.

That claim will be tested fast. GLM 5.3, released two weeks ago and covered here on the 14th, is already the incumbent open-weights coding leader on public benchmarks; Kimi K3, out in July, holds the long-context throne with a 2.8T-parameter MoE. Hy4's advantage — if it holds up — is the 1M-token context paired with an efficient 49B-active MoE, which is a workable balance of capability and inference cost. The bigger picture is that the open-weight coding tier has now had three credible new frontier releases in 45 days, all Chinese, all Apache-licensed.

For learners: pick one of these open-weight models and actually run it on a real task this week, even if only through OpenRouter. The gap between reading benchmark scores and forming a real opinion of what a model can do is bigger than most people expect, and the pace at which the frontier is shifting means an intuition built on last month's models is already stale. The models are free to try; the intuition compounds.
